newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Sweden's top Wallenberg moves as family shuffles.
newsitem.headline: Sweden's top Wallenberg moves as family shuffles.

text.p: The head of Sweden's powerful Wallenberg family, Peter Wallenberg, said on Thursday he was stepping down as chairman of investment arm Investor in the latest top management shuffles in the family empire.
Wallenberg said his decision not to stand for re-election of Investor, the family's investment vehicle, should be seen as a natural process and a generation change.
"Either I could stay on, I am 70 years old, or I could step down," Wallenberg told a news conference after the news he would step down at the annual general meeting on April 14.
"I have seen this as a business decision. We needed to have new ideas at Investor, more than anything to lead the company towards more overseas investments."
Investor said one of Sweden's top business leaders, Percy Barnevik, would succeed Wallenberg.
"We need someone with direct business contacts with people overseas," Wallenberg said.
"We judged that Percy was best.... It will be exciting to see what Percy does and if it will be any different than if a Wallenberg was chairman."
He said Barnevik would sometime in the near future leave his position of chairman at Swedish construction company Skanska but he would remain a member of the other boards in which he is involved.

Many market players had tipped Investor's current managing director Claes Dahlback to take over as chairman from Wallenberg and for the younger Marcus Wallenberg, Peter's nephew, to move into the managing director's slot.
But the older Wallenberg said the time was not right for this. Marcus, 41, is currently the vice-chief executive of Investor.
"Claes has a lot left to do in his job as managing director for Investor. Marcus also has other things to do now. We will have to wait and see what the future holds," he said.
Peter Wallenberg's eldest son, Jacob, 41, was named earlier this month as the new chief executive of S-E-Banken, to succeed Bjorn Svedberg.
S-E-Banken is viewed as a Wallenberg bank with the family owning about 18 percent of its votes and capital.
Some analysts saw the move as a precursor to the resumption of merger talks between S-E-Banken and state-controlled Nordbanken which collapsed earlier this year.
Peter Wallenberg's other son, Peter Jnr, 38, is head of the family's property and hotel company that includes Stockholm's top hotel, The Grand.
